title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 348
paragraphs: After the misfortune of his daughter, they said, a second calamity befell this king as follows. An oracle came to him from the city of Buto, saying that he was destined to live only six years more, and in the seventh he would end his life. Indignant at this, he sent a reproach to the oracle against the god, complaining in reply that whereas his father and uncle — who had shut up the temples, not only failed to remember the gods, but also destroyed men — had lived for a long time, he himself, who practiced piety, was destined to end his life so soon. And from the oracle a second message came, which said that it was for this very reason he was bringing his life to a swift close: he had not done what it was appointed for him to do, since it was destined that Egypt should suffer evils for a hundred and fifty years. The two kings before him had perceived this, but he had not. Hearing this and considering that the sentence had been passed beyond recall, Mykerinos procured a great many lamps, and whenever night came on, he lit them and began to drink and enjoy himself, stopping neither by day nor by night. He went about to the marshlands and to the woods and wherever he heard there were the most suitable places for enjoyment. He devised this — wanting to prove that the oracle spoke falsely — so that he might have twelve years of life instead of six, with the nights turned into days.
